title: Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Compounds Nscale's IPO Troubles By Walking Away From Texas Data Center Expansion - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 5, 2026 | Economy & Business, Energy, Featured, News & Analysis Nscale’s path to a public listing is narrowing as Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) declines to exercise an option that would have more than doubled their existing computing agreement at a Texas data center. Reuters reported Thursday, citing a person familiar with the matter, that the decision was made several months ago, predating Nscale’s IPO filing in September. Microsoft’s existing workflow under the original contract remains intact, and the Texas pullback does not alter the terms of the deal already in force. The two companies signed an agreement in 2025 for Nscale to deploy roughly 200,000 Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) AI chips across its data centers in both Europe and the United States. The Texas decision is the second significant retreat by Microsoft from Nscale commitments, following its exit last month from a deal to anchor Nscale’s flagship Essex, UK data center project. Power connection delays at the Essex site pushed the expected supply date into the 2030s, prompting Microsoft to walk away from that anchor arrangement entirely. Nscale, which counts Nvidia among its backers, is already under pressure from investors who have pushed back on its $130 billion IPO valuation target, according to a report published last month. The broader cloud sector is adding to the anxiety, with debt-laden neocloud operators such as CoreWeave drawing increased scrutiny amid persistent concerns about overcapacity across the industry. Political headwinds are also emerging, as the Democrats’ decisive midterm victory introduces the prospect of stricter AI regulation that could make new data center construction harder and more expensive. Separately, delays tied to IREN Ltd (NASDAQ: IREN) were cited by The Information as a factor in Microsoft spending less than it had budgeted for capital expenditures in its most recent quarter. Retail traders on Stocktwits have turned negative on the stock, with sentiment flipping to ‘bearish’ from ‘bullish,’ and one trader captured the market’s mood bluntly: “$MSFT microsoft jumped 6% today on a bet the build slows down. seems like the best ai news left is less ai spending, and a rally for not building tells you where the capex story actually stands.” Despite the turbulence, MSFT shares remain up 15.6% year to date through their last closing price, reflecting how broader market enthusiasm for AI has so far outweighed concerns about infrastructure execution. Ewan is a reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, primarily covering US current affairs and news related to NYSE-listed stocks. He has over two decades of experience in journalism and digital publishing.

title: Microsoft Stock Has Gained More Than 50% in About 4 Months. Here's What It Has Usually Done Next. - The Motley Fool
content: The software giant has run this fast 13 times before. How did the following year usually go? Microsoft (MSFT -3.58%) shares jumped nearly 7% on Wednesday, Nov. 4, as U.S. stocks rallied the day after Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections. The stock sits near $553 as of this writing. That leaves it about 57% over its June 25 close of $352.83, and the rise took just 92 trading days. A move like that is rare for a company worth about $4 trillion. But Microsoft has done it before. Going back through its daily closing prices to 1986, I find 13 past runs like this one. In 11 of them, the stock was up a year later, with a median one-year gain of around 33%. It's a solid record. But it might mean less than it seems. Microsoft stock has climbed in around 74% of all one-year periods since 1986, fast run or not. And the latest run, in July 2025, is one of the two that finished down. Every run starts the first day Microsoft closed at least 50% over its lowest close in the past 92 trading days. I used split-adjusted prices without dividends, and runs had to begin at least one year apart. "A year later" is the close 12 months after a run started (or the last trading day before it). By this rule, the current run began on Oct. 6. Ten of the 13 past runs came between 1986 and 2001, when Microsoft was a much smaller company. The biggest years came in that stretch, too. Shares more than doubled over the year after the runs that began in November 1986, January 1991, and March 1998. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. The one early miss followed a January 1988 run, when the stock was recovering from the October 1987 crash, and shares were around 12% down a year later. Since the 2001 run, Microsoft has only moved this fast three times. The stock gained around 12% over the year after June 2009 and about 33% after June 2020. Then it lost about 13% after July 2025. Even some of the good years were rough. After the January 1992 and January 2001 runs, shares slid over 20% at one point before ending the year higher. Microsoft's latest fast run hit the 50% mark the day after its fiscal 2025 fourth-quarter report on July 30, 2025. The July 31 close of $533.50 was around 50% over the April 8 low. Investors paid about 38 times earnings then, using the $14.13 a share Microsoft earned in fiscal 2025 on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis. Shares drifted mostly sideways over a few months. Then they fell all the way to that $352.83 close on June 25, 2026 -- around 34% below where the run began. Even a 15% gain the day after Microsoft's fiscal 2026 report in late July didn't erase the loss, and on July 31, 2026, shares were still about 13% down from a year earlier. I'd say the starting price mattered more than the pace of the run. At around 38 times earnings, the shares could fall a long way on any hint of trouble. In a couple of ways, I think it is. Adjusted earnings per share grew 22% in fiscal 2026, and the first quarter of fiscal 2027 (which ended Sept. 30, 2026) added another 18% gain, to $4.89. For the past four reported quarters, adjusted earnings were about $18.04 a share. At roughly $553, the stock costs about 31 times adjusted earnings, well under the 38 times earnings investors paid in July 2025. Azure, Microsoft's cloud computing platform, is also accelerating. Its revenue climbed 40% year over year in the quarter that ended September 2025, then 42% in the quarter that ended this June and 48% in the last one. Of course, that growth takes a lot of money. Microsoft's cash from operations rose 29% from a year ago. But free cash flow dropped about 27% to $18.6 billion as the company poured more cash into data centers. What has Microsoft stock usually done after a run like this? It has usually kept rising. But that record only modestly beats the stock's odds in any given year, and the most recent case went the other way. The business looks stronger than it did in July 2025, and the stock is cheaper relative to its earnings. Still, with free cash flow shrinking, paying about 31 times adjusted earnings just after a 57% run isn't something I'm eager to do. title: Election Results And Falling Oil Prices Fuel Broad Market Rally As Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) And Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Flash Buy Signals - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 5, 2026 | Economy & Business, Energy, Featured, News & Analysis, Politics A twin catalyst of election outcomes and sharply lower crude oil prices drove a powerful postelection stock market surge on Wednesday, lifting equities across a wide range of sectors. The Dow Jones Industrial Average led the charge with a gain of 3.03%, signaling strong investor confidence in the post-election economic outlook as capital rotated aggressively into blue-chip names. Oil futures told a parallel story, with the benchmark crude contract declining 0.94%, easing cost pressures for businesses and consumers alike and adding further fuel to the broader rally. While the headline indexes surged, the picture inside the technology sector was more complicated, with many tech stocks retreating even as select mega-cap names broke sharply higher. Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) posted a gain of 5.15%, with the stock flashing a clear buy signal that caught the attention of traders looking to position ahead of further postelection momentum. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) outpaced even Apple’s move, climbing 5.66% and triggering its own buy signal, reinforcing the view that institutional money was selectively rotating into the largest and most liquid technology names. Amazon also joined the group of stocks generating buy signals during the session, adding a third mega-cap name to what analysts described as a meaningful cluster of technical breakouts. Meta Platforms offered a more muted performance, gaining just 0.38%, underscoring the uneven nature of the rally even within the top tier of the technology universe. Stocks across many non-technology sectors were among the session’s clearest winners, with buy signals emerging broadly as investors responded to the combination of political clarity and lower energy costs. Market watchers cautioned, however, that at least one sector was best avoided despite the overall bullish tone, suggesting that not every corner of the market was positioned to benefit equally from the postelection environment. The divergence between the surging Dow and the mixed performance within tech highlights a broader rotation that investors will need to navigate carefully as the post-election landscape takes shape in the days ahead. David Prior is a senior reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, covering everything from current affairs and global politics to stock market news and analysis.

content: Technology stocks saw a busy week as Intel Corp. (INTC) shares plunged on a weak outlook, while Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) strong AI and cloud demand raised investor optimism. Meanwhile, Meta Platforms (META), Nvidia Corp. (NVDA), DoorDash Inc. (DASH) and Verizon Communications (VZ) announced major developments. Intel stock crashed 24% after the chipmaker issued a disappointing fourth-quarter (Q4) outlook. Although Q3 revenue climbed 21% year-on-year to $16.5 billion and adjusted earnings of $0.52 per share exceeded expectations, the company warned that supply shortages and declining PC demand would weigh on upcoming results. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the company needs to increase production to meet strong demand for its Xeon processors. Data center and AI revenue jumped 78% to $7.3 billion, while its Foundry division recorded a 58% increase to $6.7 billion. However, memory shortages and an unexpected shutdown at an Israeli facility disrupted operations. Intel expects PC demand to remain under pressure through at least the first half of 2027. For Q4, it sees revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion and adjusted earnings of $0.25 per share. RBC Capital and Goldman Sachs also reduced their price targets on Intel following the weak outlook. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock remained ‘extremely bullish’. Microsoft delivered a stronger fiscal Q1 2027 performance, with revenue up 19% to $92.3 billion and adjusted earnings of $4.89 per share. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said strong demand for the company’s AI and cloud services drove growth. Microsoft Cloud revenue rose 30% to $63.9 billion, while Azure revenue grew 48%, beating analyst estimates. However, Microsoft increased quarterly spending by 30% to $45.2 billion to build its AI infrastructure. Revenue from its consumer and devices business fell 3%. The company expects Q2 revenue of $96 billion to $97.1 billion. Baird analyst William Power raised Microsoft's price target to $600 from $500 while maintaining an ‘Outperform’ rating after the results and remains positive about faster growth in Azure and Microsoft 365. The new price target implies a 15% upside from the stock’s last close. Microsoft stock dipped 0.5% over the week, while retail sentiment around the stock slipped to ‘bullish’ from ‘extremely bullish’. Meta Platforms moved closer to its consumer robotics ambitions after developing a humanoid prototype called Max with Chinese robotics manufacturer Fourier. According to The Information’s report, the approximately 106-pound machine was developed in three months, and the companies have already started working on another version. The project is part of Meta’s plan to use AI in everyday household tasks. The company sees humanoid robots as a way to bring its Muse AI assistant into the physical world. However, U.S. restrictions and possible new limits on Chinese robotics imports could make development more difficult. Separately, Meta announced a $97.5 billion equity offering plan, including preferred and common stock sales, to support its AI infrastructure expansion and consumer AI products. Nvidia also strengthened its relationship with Meta through a $3 billion investment in the offering and an expanded AI partnership. The two companies plan to improve the training and performance of Meta's Muse platform through Nvidia's computing technology. Meta stock dropped 4% over the week with sentiment remaining ‘bearish’. DoorDash stock edged down 0.2% during the week after announcing an agreement to purchase grocery delivery platform Instacart (CART) for about $17 billion. The deal values Instacart at $65 per share, representing a 26% premium to its Oct. 22 closing price. At least 75% of the payment will consist of cash, while stock consideration will account for no more than 25%. DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said the combination could help neighborhood retailers compete with larger online businesses. The companies plan to combine DoorDash's delivery network with Instacart's grocery technology, retailer relationships and fulfillment capabilities. Retail sentiment around the stock remained ‘extremely bullish’. Verizon Communications stock had a weekly gain of 0.2% despite reporting its strongest Q3 wireless subscriber additions in five years and increasing its 2026 earnings guidance. Adjusted earnings came in at $1.31 per share, beating the $1.27 analyst estimate, although revenue of $34.31 billion missed expectations. The telecom operator added 406,000 postpaid phone customers during the quarter, more than eightfold higher than the previous year. It also generated $7.8 billion in free cash flow, up 12.1% year over year. CEO Dan Schulman addressed the potential competitive threat from SpaceX (SPCX) and its Starlink ambitions. Schulman argued that building a nationwide mobile network would require investment, thousands of cell sites and several years of work. He estimated that such an undertaking could cost between $300 billion and $500 billion over seven to eight years. Retail sentiment around the stock slipped to ‘bearish’ from ‘neutral’. So far this year, INTC, MSFT, and VZ stocks have gained between 7% and 78%, while META and DASH stocks declined 6% and 20%, respectively. Billionaire investor Mark Cuban said public companies that audited their health plans found they were being overcharged by insurers such as UnitedHealth Group (UNH), CVS Health (CVS) and Cigna (CI), but refused to tell shareholders about the findings. On a16z’s podcast on Thursday, Cost Plus Drugs co-founder Cuban said he had asked companies to run their insurance and pharmacy benefit contracts through artificial intelligence before signing them, asking where they were being overcharged and what to do about it. Cuban said a couple of the public companies that took his advice were stunned by the results. “There’s a couple public companies that I told to do this and came back to me and were like, ‘Oh my God, we had no idea how badly we were ripped off.’ I'm begging them to mention it on their quarterly earnings conference calls, and they won't do it because they still have to do business with those [insurers]," he said. Cuban did not name any companies. He supports the Break Up Big Medicine Act, which would require insurers to divest pharmacy benefit managers and provider assets. The problem starts with contracts so long that no one can catch every clause, Cuban said. He cited the city of Dallas, which has a PBM contract that tops 1,300 pages. "There's no group of humans with enough coffee on the planet to be able to catch everything they try to squeeze by," he said. He said that an insurer wins when a company signs terms it doesn't fully understand. No AI can protect it after that. Cuban said that he uses several AI agents to get contracts from school districts, cities and unions by asking for public records. He said the contracts show how these organizations are being overcharged. Cuban said that UnitedHealth has more than 3,000 subsidiaries and that these subsidiaries transfer about $150 billion a year with each other. CVS and Cigna are close behind. He said insurance companies raise premiums and deductibles and send patients to businesses they own. About 60% of people who have health insurance through their jobs get it through self-insured employers, Cuban said. He said that employers often can't figure out what they pay for and what hospitals actually get because the insurers own the administrators that process their claims. He also said insurers' earnings calls never mention lower costs for employers or patients. "They always say this is going to improve our earnings," Cuban said. UNH stock closed 0.9% lower on Friday. He said that companies should hire an executive whose only job is to handle healthcare contracts. Cuban said that the system that helps big insurers and PBMs would fall apart if employers covering about 160 million Americans ran their contracts through AI before signing. "The cost of healthcare in this country would drop like a rock," he said. CrowdStrike shares closed more than 4% lower in Friday’s regular trading session, Palo Alto Networks shares fell nearly 4%, while Okta shares fell over 6%. According to IO Fund, the first major driver behind the rally is the growing use of AI in cyberattacks and the expanding attack surface companies now have to defend. CrowdStrike’s 2026 Global Threat Report, cited by IO Fund, found that AI-enabled adversaries increased their operations by 89% in 2025. IBM’s research shows that one in four security breaches is now AI-enabled, with those incidents costing roughly $6 million on average, versus a $4.99 million global average. The threat is also pushing companies to increase spending. IO Fund cited IBM data showing that 85% of organizations plan to raise security spending after learning about the cyber capabilities of frontier AI models, up from 64% in 2025. The shift is becoming particularly important as companies deploy increasingly autonomous AI agents that can write code, access systems and perform tasks with limited human intervention. The firm also pointed to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s warning about the difficulty of securing increasingly capable AI systems: “I no longer think we’re gonna be able to just patch all the bugs,” Altman said during a speech at Stanford Graduate School of Business last month. IO Fund said Gartner expects spending on platforms designed to secure AI systems to climb from about $3 billion in 2026 to $7.7 billion in 2028, suggesting the emerging threat could translate into a substantial new security spending cycle. The other major trend identified by IO Fund is happening inside corporate security departments, which is, customers are increasingly consolidating their spending across broader cybersecurity platforms rather than buying a growing number of point solutions. CrowdStrike’s results offer one indication of the trend, the firm said, adding that CrowdStrike’s annual recurring revenue from its Falcon Flex offering topped $2.2 billion, up 101% year over year, while 51% of its subscription customers now use six or more modules. The firm added that Palo Alto Networks is seeing a similar shift. IO Fund noted that the company added roughly 220 platformization deals in its fiscal fourth quarter (Q4), more than double the pace from two years earlier. Net revenue retention among platformized customers exceeded 120%, while Prisma AIRS, its AI security platform, surpassed $100 million in annual recurring revenue. IO Fund added that AI may not simply create demand for a new category of security products, but it could also accelerate spending with vendors that can secure multiple parts of an enterprise’s infrastructure. IO Fund estimates CrowdStrike’s revenue could grow at a 23% compound annual rate through fiscal 2029, more than twice Gartner’s projected 11% annual growth for the overall cybersecurity market. Blockstream CEO Adam Back said the next big wave of Bitcoin (BTC) buying will come from professional money managers such as pension funds and insurers, adding that this phase is "still largely to come." During an interview with Bitcoin Magazine on Saturday, Back, the inventor of Hashcash, said Bitcoin's first wave of adoption came from "individuals mining or buying Bitcoin OTC or on Bitcoin exchanges." He added that "then, the ETFs brought in a second wave." Spot exchange-traded funds opened Bitcoin up to investors who were used to buying assets through a broker or financial adviser. The third wave, he said, will come through large pools of capital run by professionals. Back noted that several large investment banks have "proposed model portfolios where they would suggest 2 to 4% allocation to Bitcoin." Those allocations could flow into mutual funds that individuals pay into for long-term savings, or "be used by pension funds," he said. Back said that is how many people will end up owning Bitcoin without buying it themselves. "For most people, they are not managing their own investments," he said. Instead, their money is invested "by professional money managers in pension funds, insurance companies, life insurance policies." He added that Bitcoin treasury companies are also part of that picture, since some of those funds buy shares of publicly listed firms that hold Bitcoin. Back said regulation still limits how easily traditional institutions can hold Bitcoin. He pointed to bank capital rules, under which holding Bitcoin for clients "uses up a lot of tier one capital. So, it's quite expensive for them." He said that comes down to global Basel banking rules, which are still adapting to the asset. Back also noted that major custodians of stocks and bonds are starting to move into Bitcoin custody, helped by rule changes in the U.S. over the past year. Bitcoin's price was up 0.7% over 24 hours. (MSFT) will not exercise an option to more than double ​its existing agreement with AI cloud provider Nscale to rent more computing power at a Texas data center, Reuters reported on Thursday, citing a person familiar with the matter. The companies struck a deal last year for Nscale to deploy around 200,000 Nvidia (NVDA) AI chips with Microsoft ​across its data centers in Europe and the U.S. The reported development signals more pain for the IPO-bound Nscale. Last month, Microsoft pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's flagship data center project in ‌Essex, the UK, after ⁠power connection delays pushed its expected supply date into the 2030s. Nscale, backed by Nvidia, filed for an IPO in September, although a report last month said it faced opposition from investors over its $130 billion IPO valuation target. Reuters reported that Microsoft's decision to not expand the Texas contract was made ​several months ago, before Nscale filed for its IPO, and that its existing workflow, as per the original, was not affected. The development comes as the cloud industry faces increased scrutiny. In recent weeks, the debt-heavy model of neocloud firms such as CoreWeave has come under the scanner even as concerns prevail over overcapacity. The decisive midterm win by the Democrats, who are seen to be pro-AI regulation, has added concerns that new data centers will be harder and costlier to build. That could stifle the growth in cloud capacity essential to support AI. Meanwhile, the delays in bringing new cloud capacity online are also drawing attention. The Information reported on Wednesday that delays from IREN Ltd (IREN) contributed to Microsoft spending less than it had earmarked in capital expenditures last quarter. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for MSFT flipped to ‘bearish’ from ‘bullish.’ “$MSFT microsoft jumped 6% today on a bet the build slows down. seems like the best ai news left is less ai spending, and a rally for not building tells you where the capex story actually stands,” a trader wrote. title: Microsoft Breaks to a 52-Week High at $555.80, Up 2.27% From Its Prior Peak - 24/7 Wall St.
content: As seen on the 24/7 Wall St. homepage on November 4, 2026. Microsoft closed at $555.80, a fresh 52-week high that clears the October 13 peak by 2.27% and puts the $4.1 trillion software giant back in price discovery after a spring trough near $356. Tuesday's close at $555.80 clears the prior 52-week peak set on October 13 by 2.27%, leaving the stock with no overhead resistance from investors who bought at the top and waited to break even. Microsoft's path here ran through a spring trough near $356, and the recovery to Tuesday's close fully recaptures those losses, a turnaround few large-cap stocks manage cleanly. The quote page in one tab. Filings in another. A chart you rebuilt from scratch, a transcript you never went back and found, a screener whose settings you will redo next week. Nothing you built yesterday is still there. AlphaSpace replaces all of it with one screen you arrange yourself. Earnings calendar, estimate versus actual, the call transcript, live news, your own charts, every panel wired to whatever ticker you click. Close the browser and it is all still sitting there tomorrow. Breaking into price discovery matters for a stock carrying a $4.1 trillion valuation because institutional portfolios are sized accordingly. When a mega-cap clears a 52-week high, funds that benchmark to price levels or use technical triggers get a signal to add rather than wait, compounding buying pressure beyond what the initial move suggests. Investors who bought at the October 13 peak held underwater positions for months through the spring sell-off. With Tuesday's close above that level, those positions are now profitable, reducing the pool of motivated sellers. Retail traders are piling into the AI trade again, staying bullish on AMD, Super Micro and Microsoft, while Alphabet draws the biggest argument of the day at 346 comments. Trump Media is souring fast after the midterms, and Meta chatter is heating up. He cautions the move is only a one-day trade, with Friday's payroll report capable of undoing much of it. The leadership baton is being passed to second-tier data center names, and Cramer would rather own companies with clean balance sheets than the big caps issuing debt and equity to stay in the AI race. He is not calling a bottom yet: without a high-volume reversal day, he keeps money elsewhere. Intel tops the board on the fewest comments of the group, with 3,184 upvotes piled onto a bearish take. Big Tech names stay split ahead of earnings, Reddit's own stock is heating up, and Caterpillar chatter is souring. Four of the market's largest cash machines now spend $201.9 billion a quarter on AI buildout, so the free cash flow that funded buybacks and dividends is the line to watch next earnings season. Owning "Big Tech" as one block no longer works if only two of the group are still trending higher, with Alphabet breaking down as AI search competition pressure mounts. Voluntary exits offered to 60,000 workers put a number on the payroll-for-silicon swap funding Microsoft's AI buildout. Watch whether the labor savings land before the datacenter bill does. Microsoft chatter is heating up fast, while Amazon is the one losing the room. title: Why Did AAPL, MSFT, AMC Stocks Surge To 52-Week Highs Today? - Stocktwits
content: Apple Inc. (AAPL), Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) and AMC Entertainment Holdings Inc. (AMC) stocks surged to 52-week highs on Wednesday as a Democratic midterm election sweep and earnings momentum lifted Wall Street sentiment. Apple crossed a $5-trillion valuation, while Microsoft's stronger-than-expected earnings and 48% Azure growth fueled gains. Apple and Microsoft stocks gained 5% and 6%, respectively, while AMC Entertainment stock climbed 7%. Apple stock reached an all-time high of $354.5, taking the iPhone maker's market capitalization beyond $5 trillion. Investors responded to expectations of stronger device demand, improving cost conditions, and the company's upbeat revenue outlook. Gene Munster of Deepwater Asset Management said in an X post that slower capital spending on data centers across the technology industry could reduce pressure on memory component prices, potentially supporting Apple's future profitability. The company's December-quarter revenue forecast calls for 7% to 10% growth, ahead of Wall Street's 6% estimate. Bernstein also increased its Apple price target to $380 from $370, citing better-than-anticipated quarterly performance and encouraging revenue guidance for the first quarter of fiscal 2027. Meanwhile, Apple introduced the initial developer versions of iOS 27.3 and watchOS 27.3. The software includes new artificial intelligence capabilities for Series 12 and Ultra 4 watches, including Siri Recap. However, on Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock remained ‘bearish’. Microsoft stock also reached a record high of $559.15 on momentum from the company’s stronger-than-expected fiscal first-quarter 2027 results. Revenue increased 19% year-on-year to $92.28 billion, exceeding analyst expectations of $90.62 billion. Earnings reached $4.92 per share, comfortably ahead of the $4.71 consensus estimate. Its cloud business remained a major growth engine. Azure revenue climbed 48% to $33.17 billion, beating expectations of about 45% growth. Commercial remaining performance obligations, which represent contracted business yet to be recognized as revenue, increased 73% to $677 billion. Bill Ackman’s Pershing Square, in its Q3 letter, said that Microsoft is well positioned to profit from AI through Azure, Copilot and GitHub. The investment firm added that rising enterprise adoption, flexible pricing and expanding AI services could accelerate growth and strengthen customer relationships. Retail sentiment around the stock turned ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’. AMC stock climbed to a 52-week high of $3.56 after the company posted record results for the second straight quarter. Q3 revenue grew 31.6% to $1.71 billion, while adjusted EBITDA surged 183.7% to $347.5 million. “AMC turned audience enthusiasm into exceptional third quarter financial results thanks to our industry-leading loyalty programs along with the vast and growing number of AMC’s premium large format and extra large format auditoriums, combined with disciplined cost management, superb execution and the operating leverageinherent in our business,” said AMC CEO Adam Aron. Retail sentiment around the stock improved to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’. So far this year, AAPL, MSFT and AMC stocks have gained between 14% and 125%. (TSLA) slipped nearly 2% overnight heading into Thursday as money managers warned of political hurdles and risks to any takeover premium in a potential SpaceX merger, while Cathie Wood’s ARK Investment Management bought $47 million of SpaceX stock. TSLA shares fell 3% to $385.19 on Wednesday, bringing the week's decline to nearly 4%. Mark Tepper, CEO of Strategic Wealth Partners, cast doubt on a potential Tesla–SpaceX merger, warning that rising political pressure on Elon Musk could bring tougher regulation for both companies. “I don't see the SpaceX merger happening. Elon Musk is about to face a lot more political pressure, and that means more regulation,” he said on X. His warning followed Democrats’ takeover of both chambers of Congress and victory in the Texas governor’s race. Texas hosts major Tesla and SpaceX operations, along with their upcoming Terafab chipmaking project. XTB research director Kathleen Brooks also warned that increased congressional scrutiny could delay a transaction. “While Congress cannot stop a merger, they could slow it down via extra scrutiny,” she said. Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to study a possible merger. Gary Black, managing partner of The Future Fund, warned that an all-stock SpaceX-Tesla deal might deliver less value than bulls expect, pointing to Marvell Technology’s (MRVL) acquisition of Lumentum Holdings (LITE). “As we’ve learned (again) from $MRVL - $LITE deal, a +24% premium can quickly go negative as the acquirer’s stock is sold down,” he said on X. Black cited declines of 27% in Lumentum and 31% in Marvell from their pre-announcement levels. Earlier this week, he highlighted Lumentum’s 15% slide to $750 as Marvell fell 26% following deal rumors. Marvell’s initial offer promised 4.5 shares for each Lumentum share, worth about $1,132, a 24% premium to Lumentum’s Oct. 28 closing price. But the fixed exchange ratio means the offer’s dollar value falls alongside Marvell’s stock. With the deal expected to close in the first half of 2028, Black warned that Tesla investors could face a similarly lengthy wait. “A SPCX-TSLA deal given its size and complexity could take just as long,” he said earlier this week. Meanwhile, Cathie Wood’s ARK Investment Management bought 348,406 SpaceX shares on Wednesday, worth about $47.4 million. The ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK) led the purchases with 224,483 shares, followed by the ARK Autonomous Technology & Robotics ETF (ARKQ) with 63,478 and the ARK Next Generation Technology ETF (ARKW) with 60,445. Meanwhile, former manufacturing and supply-chain executive Jeff Lutz pushed back on concerns about Musk’s Texas projects, pointing to local approvals and economic benefits. “Every Tesla and SpaceX project went through the normal local hearings and permitting processes,” he said. Lutz estimated that Texas would account for 7% to 12% of SpaceX’s 13 gigawatts of computing capacity by the end of 2027. Musk outlined the 13-gigawatt target during last month’s earnings call. SpaceX reported 1.7 gigawatts of nameplate compute capacity as of Sept. 30. The projects have still faced local resistance. Grimes County commissioners approved Terafab’s reinvestment zone and tax incentives in June despite residents’ concerns about transparency, environmental effects, and changes to the area. Micron Technology (MU) shares tumbled to a three-month low on Wednesday amid a rout in tech stocks, triggered by Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress and calls for AI regulation. The twin victories in the House and Senate return the Democratic Party to full control of Congress for the first time since 2023. The party also flipped multiple governors’ offices in an election that serves as a rebuke to President Donald Trump. On Wednesday, Arizona Rep. Yassamin Ansari called for a pause on advanced AI development until adequate regulations are in place. “Top of the Democratic agenda on day 1 needs to be a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of this out of control industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence,” Ansari posted on X. Democrat campaigns have increasingly pushed data center operators to cover the cost of the electricity and infrastructure they use, and meet tougher environmental standards, as community opposition grows over higher power bills, heavy water use and pollution. Investors and analysts broadly expect potential new regulations from Congress to slow the rapid buildout of data centers and, in turn, constrain AI computing capacity. Micron fell 7% on Wednesday to its lowest level since early August, and another 2.2% in overnight trading, while SanDisk (SNDK) and SK Hynix (SKHY) extended their losses. Large chipmakers Nvidia (NVDA), Intel (INTC) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) fell 0.5% to 2% overnight, while neocloud stocks CoreWeave (CRWV), Nebius (NBIS) and Iren (IREN) slid between 2% and 3.6%. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) has slid 4.5% this week, and 1.2% overnight. The drops add to the pullback seen over the past month, when investors rotated out of the red of AI-linked stocks over fears of the durability of capital expenditure spending by large tech companies. Some analysts, however, sought to calm the nerves. “Spoke to a few large semiconductor and infrastructure CEOs and consensus is if the build slows in the U.S. the demand outside the U.S. is more than sufficient. Forecasts remain intact. Location is now fungible,” The Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman said in an X post. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment for MU slipped to ‘bullish’ from ‘bearish,’ while the sentiment for SNDK remained ‘extremely bullish.’ The sentiment was ‘bullish’ for NVDA and ‘extremely bullish’ for AMD and INTC. “$MU Okay so, Democrats won and now we don’t need anymore memory chips? Think twice,” a trader remarked. Another, with a contrarian view on chips, wrote: “$SOXX the rotation away from SOXX has only just started. Give it a couple more months to really get rolling." Early Uber investor and Elon Musk ally Jason Calacanis said Tesla (TSLA) and Uber Technologies (UBER) are 50% undervalued and predicted both stocks would triple in under five years as ride-sharing expands. Calacanis, who is also an All-In podcast co-host, praised Uber’s latest quarterly results and named it a top pick alongside Tesla. The call follows his $1 million in purchases of each stock last month. “Demand, growth, free cash flow and a strong position in the emerging AVs market make this my number one pick alongside $tsla right now,” he said on X. He expects ride-sharing’s share of rides to rise from about 1% to 30% within his lifetime, creating opportunities for both companies. Calacanis predicted both stocks would triple in under five years, calling them as “50% undervalued.” His latest forecast follows a separate bet on autonomous vehicle takeovers. In September, Calacanis disclosed small positions in WeRide (WRD), Pony.ai (PONY), Lucid (LCID) and Rivian (RIVN), predicting that all four would be acquired within 24 months. “Consolidation is coming to the autonomous space based on the massive progress that Tesla, Waymo, and Uber are making,” he said at the time. “I believe these four companies are going to be bought in the next 24 months and I expect, as a group, that I will 2x my investment in under two years.” He called those smaller positions as investments with a one-to-four-year horizon, compared with his usual intention to hold equities for more than a decade. Calacanis backed his bullish bet with sizable purchases. Late last month, he disclosed buying 15,000 Uber shares at $65 for $975,000 and 3,000 Tesla shares at $357 for about $1.07 million. His 12-month targets favored Uber: $120 implied 85% upside from his entry price, while Tesla’s $500 target pointed to about 40%. A $189,000 Netflix (NFLX) purchase brought the three trades to $2.24 million. Calacanis also sees room for both Uber and Tesla in autonomous driving. When asked whether Tesla’s robotaxi push threatened Uber, he predicted Tesla would capture 40% of the market, Uber and its partners 35%, and Alphabet’s Waymo 15%. Still, his enthusiasm depends on the price. “If Uber was at $100, I wouldn’t make this trade,” he said. Uber’s latest results showed strong demand and cash generation. Third-quarter gross bookings rose 20% year over year to $59.8 billion, while revenue climbed 10% to $14.77 billion. Free cash flow reached $2.54 billion for the quarter and a record $10.4 billion over the preceding 12 months. Growth still faced hurdles. Higher fuel prices and driver shortages left Mobility growth one to two percentage points below the company’s expectations. Uber is also expanding its driverless fleet, targeting about 700 vehicles on its platform by year-end and more than 2,000 by the end of 2027. It plans to launch a driverless Nuro-Lucid service in the Bay Area in early 2027, followed by supervised Rivian deployments in 2028 before moving to fully driverless operations. Meanwhile, Tesla is advancing its own service. The company said Cybercab rides began in Austin on September 3, with its robotaxi fleet reaching nearly 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles by the end of the third quarter. Beyond Tesla and Uber, Calacanis said he currently holds Netflix (NFLX), Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOG), Meta Platforms (META), Robinhood (HOOD), Nvidia (NVDA), Microsoft (MSFT), Apple (AAPL), Shopify (SHOP) and SpaceX (SPCX). “I will keep adding to these franchises and (mostly) consistent compounders due to their investments in the future, exceptional products and strong leadership,” he said. He expects these core holdings to deliver returns several times those of the index over the next decade. He also holds about 10 smaller speculative positions, which he would cut if their products and business fundamentals stopped improving. (IREN) drew attention from retail traders on Wednesday as cloud and AI stocks came under pressure after Democrats won the midterm elections. The Australian data center company also faced scrutiny after a report said it contributed to Microsoft’s lower AI capital spending last quarter. IREN shares fell 2.5% in overnight trading, after a 11.4% drop in the regular session. Notably, IREN is scheduled to report its fiscal first-quarter results after the markets close on Thursday. The Information reported, citing unnamed sources, that IREN faced delays at the Childress, Texas data center site, leading Microsoft to delay spending it had slated for the September quarter. Microsoft spent about $5 billion less on capital expenditures than planned last quarter because data center capacity it expected to rent wasn’t ready on time. “Capital expenditures were $45.2 billion as some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed,” Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said in the analyst call last week. One provider involved is Iren, though it is unclear how much its delay contributed to the shortfall, according to The Information’s report. Microsoft had agreed to spend $9.7 billion over five years renting Nvidia-powered servers at Iren’s Childress, Texas, data center. Iren had planned to bring the servers online gradually through 2026, but has been facing delays. Stocks tied to data centers fell Wednesday as investors expect slower AI buildout after Democrats win Congress. Investors and analysts believe that Democrats would tighten regulations for data centers, effectively slowing the buildout of AI infrastructure. Data center stocks plunged: CoreWeave (CRWV) and Core Scientific (CORZ) fell 10% each while Nebius and Applied Digital fell 7% each , with all four falling further in overnight trading. IREN stocks have fallen sharply after hitting a record high last November, and investors are looking for signs of revival. Analysts expect sales to fall 9% to $221.7 million in its fiscal first quarter, which would mark the third consecutive degrowth in sales in a row, per Koyfin. They expected adjusted loss to be $0.67 per share, sharply higher than $0.01 per share loss in the corresponding quarter a year ago. title: MSFT Stock Surges Above $555 to New Record Highs as Midterms Lift Microsoft and Big Tech - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft stock has rallied above $555 to a new record after recovering from a decline toward $500, as strong cloud growth and improving sentiment following the U.S. midterm elections support buyers, despite growing scrutiny of infrastructure spending and future computing commitments. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares have staged a sharp recovery after falling toward $500, with the stock extending its gains today to break above $557 and establish a new record high. The rebound follows renewed concerns about the company’s relationship with Anthropic, rising infrastructure costs and the substantial investment required to expand its computing capacity. Improving sentiment across technology stocks following the U.S. midterm elections has provided another catalyst. Investors are reassessing the potential impact of political pressure on data-centre construction, particularly as electricity costs, grid stability and water consumption become increasingly important issues. Greater regulatory scrutiny could force hyperscalers to reconsider the pace of infrastructure expansion. Although this could create operational challenges, investors may also view more disciplined spending as positive for free cash flow, which has become a major concern across the technology sector. The removal of election uncertainty has also allowed markets to refocus on corporate earnings, economic conditions and the outlook for large technology companies. However, the implications of the election results for tariffs, fiscal negotiations and government policy remain uncertain. Microsoft’s latest quarterly results demonstrated continued strength across its core operations. Net income increased 32% year-over-year to $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, excluding the impact of investments in OpenAI. Revenue increased to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier, while earnings comfortably exceeded the analyst consensus of $4.27 per share. Despite the strong performance, the market reaction highlighted a growing distinction between earnings growth and the returns generated from infrastructure investment. Investors are increasingly questioning whether Microsoft’s spending commitments can translate into sustainable profitability and sufficient cash generation. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year-over-year, or 31% in constant currency. The performance highlights continued demand for cloud computing services and Microsoft’s ability to attract enterprise customers. Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said the company exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income and earnings per share. CEO Satya Nadella also highlighted improvements in computing capacity, customer choice, security and cost efficiency. Nevertheless, expanding cloud capacity requires substantial investment in data centres, servers, networking equipment and specialised processors. The challenge is ensuring that revenue growth keeps pace with capital expenditure rather than allowing infrastructure costs to weaken margins and free cash flow. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months which has now turned into a support zone, and climbed above $550 earlier in October but slipped toward $500 again on Monday. The price slip breached the 50 daily SMA in September which has been acting as support and we’re seeing a rebound today. The price has now pushed to a new record high above $555 area which represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MAFT buyers gave up at this zone, revering lower. An amended filing concerning Microsoft’s relationship with Anthropic identifies at least $44.9 billion in commitments to Microsoft through June 2033, subject to contractual delivery and breach provisions. The disclosure relates to an existing arrangement amended during 2026 and highlights the scale of future computing demand. However, large commitments do not eliminate the risks associated with financing and infrastructure expansion. Smaller cloud providers could face greater pressure if borrowing costs remain elevated or customer demand fails to meet expectations. Recent warnings from Elon Musk about the sustainability of some infrastructure businesses have added to concerns about debt-funded data-centre construction. Microsoft has a stronger financial position than many smaller competitors, but it still needs to demonstrate that these commitments will generate attractive returns. Microsoft is also investing in its Maia 300 processor to improve computing efficiency and reduce dependence on external chip suppliers. The processor reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver significantly higher rack-scale throughput than Maia 200. Custom silicon could eventually reduce computing costs and improve infrastructure efficiency. However, development, deployment and scaling require substantial investment before those benefits become fully visible. Microsoft has also reportedly discussed leasing computing capacity from SpaceX, although the status of those discussions remains unclear. Not every division is experiencing the same momentum. Microsoft’s Devices and Consumer segment generated $15.5 billion in revenue, down 3% year-over-year. Search and advertising revenue increased 12%, but Xbox content and services revenue declined 2%, while Windows OEM and Devices revenue fell 22%. Regulatory pressure also remains a consideration. The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority has proposed designating Microsoft as having strategic market status in certain software markets, potentially increasing scrutiny of licensing, pricing and product bundling. Competition from Google Workspace could add further pressure as businesses reassess subscription costs and available alternatives. The move above $557 marks a significant recovery from the recent decline toward $500. Strong earnings, 30% Microsoft Cloud growth and substantial future computing demand continue to support the company’s fundamentals. However, the central question remains whether Microsoft’s infrastructure commitments and custom-chip investments can deliver sufficient returns. The latest rally suggests buyers are regaining confidence, but elevated spending, financing risks and regulatory scrutiny remain important considerations as the stock enters record territory.

Zhitong Finance APP learned that as the AI lab has signed contracts to use a significant portion of the under-construction AI computing capacity, market concerns about customer concentration risk continue to mount. In this report, Bernstein uses OpenAI's annual contract commitments as a proxy for all AI labs and arrives at a conclusion contrary to the panic narrative: although the commitment scale is large, it is tiered over time and not entirely irrevocable; as capacity and related costs grow, so do OpenAI's leverage and payment capabilities—meaning that for major suppliers such as Oracle (ORCL.US) and Microsoft (MSFT.US), downside risk is low. Bernstein maintains an "Outperform" rating on Microsoft and Oracle (with price targets of $722 and $325, respectively) and an "Underperform" rating on CoreWeave (with a price target of $54): It has no concerns about its existing backlog but doubts its ability to renew contracts and secure additional deals with strong economics. Bernstein first clarifies the narrative: the media claim that "OpenAI has committed over $1.5 trillion" reflects a long-term vision rather than a specific contract. Two more reliable data points are as follows: in October 2025, OpenAI stated that Stargate had secured nearly 7 GW of planned capacity, with investments exceeding $400 billion over the next three years, and had already locked in commitments for $500 billion and 10 GW by the end of 2025; a July 2026 report, meanwhile, estimated OpenAI's cloud-computing infrastructure spending through 2030 at approximately $750 billion. Bernstein's bottom-up model estimates that, assuming all contracts are delivered on time—which the report explicitly calls "highly unlikely"—OpenAI's infrastructure spending through 2030 would total approximately $614 billion; on an annual basis, the peak of currently committed spending occurs in 2031 at about $184 billion. Signing a $750 billion contract does not equate to paying out $750 billion in cash before 2030 for three reasons: First, chips from NVIDIA, Broadcom, and AMD will likely be financed by suppliers and paid for over roughly six years based on the hardware's lifespan, with delivery schedules and quantities remaining uncertain; second, agreements with AMD and Cerebras include warrants that vest in tiers tied to AMD's stock price, meaning these chips could effectively cost OpenAI little or nothing depending on share-price movements; third, the self-built Project Camellia data-center shell—roughly $20 billion, 3.2 gigawatts in Georgia, phased into operation from 2028 to 2032—is a long-lived asset that could have been capitalized over time or financed differently, but the report treats it as a front-loaded expense. Key demand-side data: According to the report, OpenAI told investors that its annualized revenue at the end of September was close to $50 billion, with total revenue up 77% year over year. Extrapolating from this, OpenAI's revenue next year would exceed $80 billion, surpassing the report's estimate for infrastructure spending in 2027 (excluding the $15 billion Camellia supercomputer). The report projects that OpenAI's infrastructure spending will grow about 58% year over year in 2028 to $139 billion (or $129 billion excluding the supercomputer). As long as revenue growth remains at or above 60%, revenue is expected to continue outpacing infrastructure spending. Bernstein notes that OpenAI has consistently exceeded its revenue targets in every reporting period; at the industry level, global annual inference spending ultimately needs to reach five to twenty times training spending, and we are still in the early stages. Oracle's relationship with OpenAI centers on a $300 billion deal, comprising multiple tranches of 5- to 6-year capacity contracts (signed in 2025, effective from 2026, rolling out through 2030, with Bernstein expecting the bulk to occur in 2028). Bernstein estimates Oracle can recognize approximately $312 billion in revenue, with 57% booked before its fiscal year 2030; OpenAI accounts for less than 50% of Oracle's RPO, and this share will continue to decline as other businesses grow. Microsoft's relationship with OpenAI is complex: as an investor, model user, and capacity supplier, Microsoft previously announced that OpenAI has contracted to purchase an additional $250 billion in Azure services, with each tranche structured as a 6-year contract aligned with hardware lifecycles. Amazon has two agreements: a $38 billion, 7-year deal signed in 2025, and a $100 billion, 8-year agreement signed in 2026 as part of their collaboration (including up to 2 GW of Trainium chips). CoreWeave (CRWV.US) has contracts with OpenAI totaling approximately $22.4 billion ($11.9 billion signed in March 2025 along with a $350 million equity investment, $4 billion in May, and up to $6.5 billion in September), but Bernstein emphasizes that the contract language specifies "caps" rather than committed revenue. Although Google (GOOGL.US) has been repeatedly rumored to have capacity and TPU agreements with OpenAI, it lacks contractual evidence verifiable in financial reports, leading Bernstein to exclude it from the model. The report specifically cites two canceled cases: OpenAI had reached an agreement with Oracle to expand the Abilene 2.1 GW project in Texas, but later withdrew and ceded the adjacent 900 MW site to Microsoft/Crusoe; the developer Crusoe found a replacement tenant within about two weeks. Similarly, after OpenAI pulled out of the Stargate project in Norway (a collaboration between Nscale and Aker) announced in July, Microsoft took over. These examples illustrate a significant gap between "announcements" and "irrevocable contracts." Bernstein judges that AI labs are pushing ahead with capacity far exceeding actual needs, and a normalization of supply and demand may occur within the next two to three years. The real risk to the industry lies not in the scale of commitments made by leading labs, but in speculative construction and low-quality business models spurred by the easing of capacity scarcity. Bernstein reiterated its skepticism about neocloud's business model, believing that labs will increasingly rely on hyperscale cloud partnerships, hosting agreements, and self-built infrastructure. content: Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ: MSFT) announced that Emma N. Walmsley has notified the board of directors of her decision not to stand for re-election at the company’s annual shareholders meeting on Dec. 8, 2026. This follows the announcement earlier today by HP Inc. that she will become their CEO, effective Jan. 4, 2027. “We are grateful to Emma for her contributions to Microsoft and the industry expertise, thoughtful judgment, and global perspective she brought to our board,” said Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft. “We look forward to continuing our partnership with Emma and with HP.” Sandi Peterson, the company’s lead independent director, said, “Emma brought a valuable and distinct perspective to our board, combining her global business expertise with a balanced perspective and sound judgment. It has been a privilege to serve with her.” Ms. Walmsley has served as a Microsoft director since 2019, currently sitting on the Compensation and Environmental, Social, and Public Policy committees. Her experience and engagement contributed to the success of the company on a broad range of issues throughout her board service. The result reinforced its position as one of the most closely watched names in US Technology Stocks, with cloud and artificial intelligence services once again doing most of the work. The headline figure was Azure, the company's cloud platform, which grew even faster than in the prior quarter. Management said demand continues to exceed available capacity, a message that suggests the AI build-out has further to run. Azure is now Microsoft's single biggest business line, a remarkable shift for a company once defined by Windows and Office. Growth accelerated on demand for AI training and inference workloads, along with steady migration of traditional enterprise applications to the cloud. The broader Microsoft Cloud division also accelerated. Management described a fast start to the fiscal year and pointed to customers committing to larger, longer contracts. Commercial productivity cloud revenue continued to grow steadily, helped by the rollout of AI assistants across productivity software. The commercial remaining performance obligation, a measure of contracted revenue not yet recognised, surged to a record. This backlog provides unusual visibility and shows that customers are locking in cloud and AI capacity for years ahead rather than paying for short-term needs. Microsoft reorganised its reporting into an Agents and Infra unit, which captures much of the cloud and AI business, and a Devices and Consumer unit. The infrastructure side grew strongly, while devices and consumer revenue slipped, reflecting softer demand for Windows hardware and gaming. The new structure makes the company's priorities clear. Most incremental revenue and profit now comes from cloud infrastructure and AI agents sold to enterprises, while consumer products play a supporting role. To meet demand, Microsoft continues to invest heavily in data centers, chips and networking. Capital expenditures roughly doubled from a year earlier, and management signalled a large spending plan for the full fiscal year. Unlike some peers, Microsoft's operating cash flow still comfortably covers this investment. Reported profit was also boosted by gains linked to its investment in a leading AI model developer, which widened the gap between reported and adjusted growth. Investors generally focus on adjusted figures for a cleaner view of underlying performance. Guidance pointed to continued strong growth in the coming quarter, with Azure expected to grow at a similar or slightly faster pace in constant currency. Management again said capacity constraints remain, meaning revenue growth is partly limited by how quickly new data centers come online. That is an unusual position for a company of Microsoft's scale. It implies demand is not the bottleneck; supply is. As new facilities open, the company expects to convert more of its backlog into revenue. The scale of investment is the main concern. If AI demand slows, or pricing for AI services falls faster than expected, returns on new data centers may disappoint. Power availability, chip supply and regulatory scrutiny of large technology platforms are further factors to monitor. Competition is also intensifying. Rival cloud platforms reported strong growth this season, and custom chips from cloud providers are changing the economics of AI infrastructure. Microsoft's broad enterprise relationships remain a powerful advantage, but no platform has the market to itself. Beyond infrastructure, Microsoft is pushing AI agents into everyday business software. Tools that draft documents, summarise meetings and automate routine tasks are being bundled into enterprise subscriptions, giving the company new ways to raise revenue per user. Adoption across large organisations is still building, but management sees it as a long-term growth layer on top of the cloud. Developer tools and security products also benefit from AI features, strengthening the overall ecosystem and making it harder for customers to switch providers once their workflows are built around Microsoft platforms. The partnership with a leading AI model developer remains a significant strategic asset. It gives Microsoft early access to advanced models for its cloud and software products, while the developer relies on Azure capacity for training and serving its systems, deepening ties between the two organisations. As a heavyweight in the Nasdaq Composite, Microsoft's results help set the tone for the entire technology sector. This quarter offered reassurance that enterprise demand for cloud and AI services remains robust, even as markets debate the overall size of AI spending. The next reports are likely to focus on how quickly capacity expands, whether Azure growth stays near current levels and how AI assistants translate into broader software revenue. For now, the company enters its fiscal year with clear momentum. The companies said they are expanding a collaboration so that their sales teams can pursue enterprise customers together where network modernization, migration to Azure and AI adoption overlap. AI systems are only as useful as the data they can reach. Large organisations typically keep information in several public clouds, in private data centres, in branch offices and in partner environments, and the links between those places were often built a project at a time. The announcement describes that patchwork as fragmented and complex, and treats it as a brake on AI deployment. Lumen said it plans to make its cloud networking and application connectivity suite available through Microsoft's cloud and AI ecosystem. Dem. James Talarico won the state's Senate seat, defeating Rep. Ken Paxton. Her proposals include requiring data centers to pay for transmission infrastructure, screening projects for grid impacts, ending tax breaks and giving communities more say. She has repeated the calls during her campaign. Investors and analysts believe a pause or added costs could slow new data center construction and, in turn, constrain AI computing capacity. They fear that a major Democratic win could strengthen the growing nationwide push for data center restrictions. Texas is home to data centers operated by Google, AWS, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle, as well as AI campuses developed by Crusoe for customers including OpenAI, Oracle, Microsoft and Google. title: PLTR Stock Gets Fresh Price Target Hikes, But Jefferies Favors MSFT, ORCL, SNOW Shares - Stocktwits
content: Palantir Technologies (PLTR) shares fell in morning trading on Tuesday, putting the stock on track to hit its lowest level since September, even as analysts raised their price targets following the company’s third-quarter results. Citi, Morgan Stanley, Piper Sandler and RBC Capital all lifted their targets, but Jefferies kept its target steady at $80 with an ‘Underperform’ rating, according to TheFly. The firm said that while Palantir delivered a "strong" quarter, the debate has shifted from whether customers want Palantir’s software to whether the company can sustain accelerating growth against tougher comparisons. Jefferies said it sees “more compelling” risk and reward elsewhere in Microsoft (MSFT), Oracle (ORCL), and Snowflake (SNOW). According to the firm, they offer strong long-term growth at more attractive valuations. PLTR stock dropped around 5% in morning trade and was among the top-trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing. Palantir reported revenue growth accelerating for the 13th consecutive quarter. Revenue grew 96% year over year in the third quarter (Q3) to $2.31 billion, beating market expectations of $2.17 billion, according to Koyfin. The company also raised its full-year revenue forecast to $8.53 billion from about $8.15 billion, its third increase this year. It expects fourth-quarter (Q4) revenue of about $2.65 billion. Citi, which raised its target to $265 from $250 and kept a ‘Buy’ rating, called the results “another top-line blowout,” driven by U.S. commercial and government sales. Morgan Stanley analyst Sanjit Singh called revenue growth for a 13th consecutive quarter “impressive.” The main concern for Wall Street was bookings, which indicate future business. Total contract value (TCV), which measures the value of deals signed during the quarter, rose 6% year over year to $2.92 billion, down sharply from 49% growth in the second quarter. U.S. commercial TCV increased 11%. According to Morgan Stanley, PLTR stock’s reaction reflected elevated expectations for U.S. commercial sales and slower bookings growth linked to shorter contracts. Meanwhile, RBC Capital highlighted remaining deal value grew just 2% from the second quarter, while remaining performance obligations (RPO) were flat sequentially. The firm also noted management’s acknowledgment that contracts tied to Sovereign AI, Palantir’s work with national governments, were shorter than usual. Piper Sandler said investors will look for evidence in coming quarters that the 11% growth in U.S. commercial bookings “is a fluke of duration and not something structural.” The firm believes the slowdown is related to contract length and said demand for Palantir’s software still “very much outstrip[s] supply.” Citi also described the quarter as strong “despite a duration headwind to bookings.” On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around PLTR stock flipped to ‘bullish’ from ‘bearish’ over the past day, while chatter increased to ‘extremely high’ from ‘normal’ levels. Platform data showed an over 1,100% increase in message volume over the past 24 hours. Some retail traders pushed back against concerns over Palantir's valuation and growth outlook, with some pointing to what they saw as a shift in the criticism of Palantir's business mix. If the PLTR stock's decline holds through the regular session, the shares would give up their year-to-date gains. Meanwhile, Tesla continued its European recovery, with October vehicle registrations surging 248% in Sweden, 131% in Norway and 34% in Denmark, according to Reuters. Registrations also climbed 271% in Spain, 186% in Portugal and 94% in Italy. The rebound was supported by higher fuel prices, government incentives and rising EV demand, the report read. While Tesla emerged as Norway’s top-selling brand in October, competition remained intense in Denmark, where it was outperformed by Chinese rivals BYD, Leapmotor, Xpeng and MG. Tesla’s Shanghai factory has an installed annual production capacity exceeding 950,000 vehicles, making it one of the company’s most important manufacturing and export hubs. However, the facility is in the spotlight due to potential complications in the merger between Tesla and SpaceX (SPCX). Last week, Bank of America flagged China as the biggest regulatory risk to the proposed combination, as the merger would bring Tesla’s Shanghai operations under the ownership of a major U.S. defense contractor. Veteran market strategist Ed Yardeni warned Monday that a Democratic sweep in Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections could deliver a “cold shower for stocks,” arguing that investors have yet to fully price in that possibility. Yardeni said political gridlock could become damaging paralysis, complicating government spending and debt-ceiling negotiations. Prolonged fiscal standoffs could push Treasury yields higher and weigh on equity valuations, he added. He also argued that a Democratic-controlled Congress might do little to constrain President Donald Trump's use of executive authority, citing tariffs and military action against Iran. However, Yardeni said he would view a significant market selloff as a buying opportunity, given the strength of the U.S. economy and corporate earnings. UBS Global Wealth Management assigned a 50% probability to a Democratic sweep, a 40% chance of Democrats winning the House while Republicans retain the Senate, and a 10% probability of Republicans retaining both chambers. In its Monday report, UBS said changes in congressional control could complicate fiscal negotiations, with debt-ceiling discussions in 2027 potentially creating volatility. However, the bank said that narrow congressional majorities and presidential veto power should limit sweeping legislation, while Trump would retain considerable authority over tariffs, foreign policy, and regulation. UBS also expects Treasury yields to settle slightly lower over the next 12 months as easing inflation should outweigh persistent fiscal concerns. The bank said it “would not treat the midterms as a binary directional event” for markets, emphasizing that earnings, economic growth, AI investment and interest rates remain more important drivers. The election also comes amid a pullback in AI stocks. However, UBS does not expect a change in congressional control to derail data-center expansion, as many relevant decisions are made at state and local levels. According to a Reuters report, Citigroup U.S. equity strategist Scott Chronert said stocks would likely react positively if Republicans retained control of the Senate, but negatively if Democrats secured a larger-than-expected Senate majority. “Investors are going into the midterms very cautious,” Indosuez Wealth Management Chief Investment Officer Alexandre Drabowicz told Bloomberg, adding that market fundamentals remain strong and the S&P 500 has historically resumed climbing after elections. BlackRock's Oct.1 research highlighted growing scrutiny of AI infrastructure, citing local ballot measures seeking data-center moratoriums in Ohio, increased construction auditing in Texas, and Virginia's proposed framework supporting data centers' own power supplies. Yorkville Advisors partner and managing director Dan Ives on Tuesday called the prospect of Anthropic (ANT) receiving a below-investment-grade credit rating “a bit of a gut punch,” and that the Claude-maker’s valuation could fall below $1.5 trillion by mid-November. “The investment grade.. that’s something of a gut punch,” Ives said in an interview with Bloomberg. His comments came after the Financial Times reported last week that Blackstone told investors the company was likely to receive a rating in the double-B range after its IPO, which would put it below investment grade, in a category commonly known as “junk.” On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around ANT stock, yet to go public, trended in ‘bearish’ territory at the time of writing. Anthropic’s amended IPO filing, released on Monday, disclosed $895.4 billion in commitments, largely tied to computing capacity and data centers. About $447.5 billion of those commitments are expected to come in before the end of 2030. A below-investment-grade rating typically means higher borrowing costs and can limit demand from bond funds that face restrictions on holding lower-rated debt. That could make it more expensive for Anthropic to finance its commitments. “I think it will be tougher,” Ives said on whether the investment rating could make it harder for Anthropic to meet those obligations. Amazon (AMZN)-backed Anthropic, the maker of Claude, has reportedly seen its target IPO valuation fall from roughly $2 trillion to between $1.5 trillion and $1.6 trillion. Ives said the lower range may not be the bottom, given how much capital the company is expected to need. “The amount of capital that they’re going to need to raise, and you could call it 1.5, is maybe baseline to what probably could even go lower by mid-November,” he stated. Ives said uncertainty around Anthropic had weighed on technology stocks because the company is central to the AI ecosystem, with ties to major chipmakers and cloud providers. “I think that definitely put pressure on the tech trade because Anthropic, it’s foundational to the AI revolution. No matter which way you cut it, from Nvidia to Microsoft to Amazon to everything,” he said. “So, the tech trade needs this to go public.” He also warned that semiconductor stocks could face further losses after their recent decline. According to him, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) could drop “another 10 to 12%.” Ives added that investors are becoming less willing to tolerate heavy AI spending without evidence that it will generate revenue. Companies that may once have had 12 to 18 months to demonstrate returns could now have just six to nine months, he said. Ives said the industry may need to impose limits on borrowing and data-center expansion, pointing to Oracle (ORCL) as a potential example. “I think there’s a line in the sand. I think Oracle would probably be more the poster child,” he said. Companies may need to decide how much capital they are willing to raise and stick to that limit, he added. title: Bill Ackman on MSFT, AMZN and META: Why Big Tech's Trillion-Dollar AI Spend Is 'Offensive Rather Than Defensive' - TradingView
content: Bill Ackman‘s Pershing Square Inc. PS has said that the artificial intelligence (AI) capital expenditures by Microsoft Corp. MSFT, Amazon.com Inc. AMZN, and Meta Platforms Inc. META are designed to accelerate growth. In a recent shareholder letter, the executives described the projected trillion-dollar outlay by major technology companies as “offensive rather than defensive.” Addressing investor concerns regarding the returns on elevated spending by the hyperscalers, Chief Executive Officer William Ackman and Chief Investment Officer Ryan Israel wrote, “We believe that the hyperscalers’ capital spending is offensive rather than defensive.” The executives stated that “Rather than merely protecting existing franchises, we believe the hyperscalers are investing to accelerate growth and are deploying capital behind a transformative technology that plays directly to their competitive advantages.” The letter detailed how these investments are impacting specific portfolio companies. Regarding AMZN, the executives wrote that “Amazon is extremely well positioned across the AI stack.” They noted that “AI has helped AWS accelerate its revenue growth to 39% in the third quarter.” For META, the letter stated that “Meta’s core digital advertising business has effectively used AI for better ad targeting, generative ad copy, and more effective content recommendation.” Ackman and Israel also noted, “By frontloading its compute investment, Meta has given itself the optionality to scale Muse to a billion or more users.” Regarding MSFT, the executives stated, “Microsoft occupies an enviable position among the hyperscalers in having two large channels by which to monetize its compute.” They noted that “the narrative on the stock has shifted from the company being an AI laggard to an AI leader.” Beyond the hyperscalers, Ackman and Israel highlighted what they view as mispriced opportunities in other portfolio companies. Regarding Uber Technologies Inc. UBER, the executives noted the stock now trades at “its lowest valuation ever.” They stated that investor concerns regarding autonomous vehicles are “increasingly disconnected from its strong business performance.” Ackman and Israel wrote that “the risk due to AVs is minimal,” and projected that Uber’s earnings per share will “compound at 25% or more for the foreseeable future.” Addressing Netflix Inc. NFLX, the letter noted that recent stock declines were driven by investor concerns over plateauing engagement. However, the executives argued that measuring engagement solely by watch time “overshadows the quality of that engagement, which is what ultimately drives the value proposition for Netflix subscribers.” Ackman and Israel concluded that the market “vastly undervalues the company’s growth profile and business quality.” The letter acknowledged concerns over how these companies will fund their infrastructure buildout.
